questions.source: Drill P1 — 1819 final Q8a (ARP, same subnet)
questions.prompt: PCA (192.168.1.111) must send to PCB (192.168.1.115) on the **same subnet**; PCA's ARP table is empty. What is the **destination MAC of PCA's ARP query**?
options: FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF — broadcast, so all LAN1 nodes receive it
The router's MAC 6A-12-55-34-55-55
00-00-00-00-00-00 — unknown placeholder
questions.explain:
ARP process (4 marks):
1. PCA checks 192.168.1.115 against its mask → **same subnet** → needs **PCB's MAC** directly.
2. Not in the (empty) ARP table → PCA **broadcasts an ARP query** containing PCB's IP; dst MAC = **FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF**.
3. Only **PCB replies**, unicast to PCA's MAC, carrying 31-13-33-33-45-56.
4. PCA **caches** the mapping (TTL ≈ 20 min) and sends the frame.

questions.source: Drill P2 — 1819 final Q8b (ARP, different subnet)
questions.prompt: PCA must send to PCC (**different subnet**, behind router R1). Whose MAC does PCA actually need?
options: R1 int1's MAC (the default gateway) — a frame cannot cross a router
PCC's MAC — ARP works end-to-end
R1 int2's MAC (the far interface)
No MAC needed — IP handles it
questions.explain:
Different subnet → the frame goes to PCA's **default gateway, R1 int1**. PCA ARPs for **192.168.1.1** and gets 6A-12-55-34-55-55.
**MAC addresses only have meaning on the local LAN** — the datagram inside still carries dst IP = 192.168.55.222 (PCC); R1 re-ARPs on LAN2.

questions.prompt:
Datagram PCA→PCC crossing R1. On **LAN2 (R1→PCC)**, which addresses does the frame carry?

(PCA=01-12-…-56, R1 int1=6A-…-55, R1 int2=9A-…-58, PCC=62-FE-…-A3)
options: src IP 192.168.55.1 · dst IP 192.168.55.222 · src MAC 9A-… · dst MAC 62-FE-…
src IP 192.168.1.111 · dst IP 192.168.55.1 · src MAC 6A-… · dst MAC 9A-…
questions.explain:
**Rule: IP addresses never change in transit; MAC addresses are rewritten at every hop.**

| Location | src IP | dst IP | src MAC | dst MAC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X (PCA→R1, LAN1) | 192.168.1.111 | 192.168.55.222 | PCA 01-12-… | **R1 int1 6A-…** |
| Y (R1→PCC, LAN2) | 192.168.1.111 | 192.168.55.222 | **R1 int2 9A-…** | PCC 62-FE-… |

questions.prompt: PCC (LAN2) has been sending to PCD (same LAN) and PCB (other LAN). PCC's ARP table contains:
options: PCD's entry + R1 int2's entry (192.168.55.1) — never PCB's MAC
PCD's entry + PCB's entry
PCB, PCD and both router interfaces
Only PCD's entry
questions.explain: Same subnet → direct entry (PCD → 7C-BA-B2-B4-91-10). Other subnet → entry for the **router interface on PCC's side** (R1 int2, 192.168.55.1 → 9A-12-66-34-75-58). An ARP table NEVER holds MACs from another LAN.

questions.prompt: Switch table initially **empty**; hosts A–F on ports 1–6. **C sends a frame to A.** What does the switch do?
options: Learns (C, port 3); FLOODS the frame on every port except 3 — A's location is unknown
Learns (A, port 1); forwards on port 1 only
Drops the frame — destination unknown
Learns (C, port 3); forwards on port 1 only
questions.explain:
Self-learning: the switch records the **SOURCE** (C, 3). The destination A is **unknown → flood** all ports except the arrival port.
Next events: A→C is **selective forward to port 3 only** (C now known) and the switch learns (A,1); F→A forwards on **1 only**; etc.
Marking pattern: 1 mark per learned entry, 1 per correct forwarding decision + justification.

questions.prompt: Sender data **D = 100100**, generator **G = 1101**, r = 3. Compute the CRC remainder **R** (3 bits).
Receiver gets **100100001** and divides by G = 1101. The remainder is **000**. Verdict?
options: No error detected — the frame is accepted
Error detected — the frame is rejected
Cannot tell without the original data
The receiver must request the generator first
questions.explain:
Receiver divides the WHOLE received string by G: **remainder 000 → no error detected; accept.** (It is exactly the P5 transmission.)
Contrast P6(b): received 100000001 → remainder **011 ≠ 0 → error detected; reject**.
Marking (5m): setup 1, visible XOR steps 2, remainder 1, verdict stated 1.

questions.prompt: In the received 2-D even-parity block, **row 2 has five 1s (parity fails)** and **column 5 has three 1s (parity fails)**. What does the receiver conclude?
options: Single-bit error at (row 2, column 5) — flip it: received 1, corrected to 0
Two errors — discard the block
The parity row itself is corrupt
Error at (row 5, column 2)
questions.explain: 2-D parity can **detect AND CORRECT a single-bit error**: the failing row × failing column intersect at the bad bit → **(row 2, col 5): 1 → 0**. Single-bit parity can only detect (odd numbers of) errors — that's the advantage sentence worth a mark.

questions.prompt: Arrange the **CSMA/CD** steps in order (Ethernet NIC):
items: Sense the channel; if idle, transmit the entire frame; if busy, defer
While transmitting, listen for other transmissions
On detecting a collision: abort immediately and send a JAM signal
Pick K from {0,1,…,2^m − 1} and wait K × 512 bit times (binary exponential backoff)
Return to carrier sensing and retry
questions.explain:
CSMA/CD = **carrier sense** (listen before) + **collision detection** (listen WHILE transmitting).
Collision → **abort early + jam** (everyone learns; channel wastage cut short) → **binary exponential backoff**: after the m-th collision, K ∈ {0…2^m−1}, wait **K × 512 bit times** — more collisions ⇒ wider window ⇒ adaptively lighter load.
Collisions exist at all because of **propagation delay**.

questions.source: Drill P8 close — CD vs wireless
questions.prompt: Why does collision **detection** work on wired Ethernet but **not** on wireless?
options: Wired NICs can compare transmitted vs received signal; in wireless your own transmission overwhelms the received signal, and hidden terminals make some collisions undetectable
Radio waves travel too fast to detect
Wireless frames have no addresses
Wireless uses TCP instead of CSMA
questions.explain: On a wire you can detect a collision by comparing signal strengths. A wireless sender is deaf while transmitting (its own signal drowns everything) and **hidden terminals** mean a collision at the receiver may be physically invisible at the sender — hence 802.11 uses **CSMA/CA** (avoidance + ACKs) instead.
